item.title: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office: Patent Backlog Reduction Efforts Pose Risks to Examiner Retention and Examination Quality
item.description:
What GAO Found
The backlog of unexamined patent applications awaiting an initial decision from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) rose to about 838,000 applications in January 2025. In September 2025, the USPTO announced a goal to reduce the backlog to under 599,000 applications but did not specify a time frame for reaching it. The backlog was last at that level in 2020. To reduce the backlog, the USPTO is requiring patent examiners to review more applications, has decreased examiner training, and has expanded the use of AI patent search tools. As of August 2026, the USPTO reduced the backlog to about 756,000 applications, but average applicant wait times for a final patentability decision had increased by 11 percent since January 2025.
GAO’s analysis found that, even with examiners doing more work, the USPTO is unlikely to reduce the backlog to under 599,000 patent applications before 2031 without lowering examiner attrition (see figure). The examiner attrition rate increased from 2.9 percent in fiscal year 2020 to 7.6 percent in fiscal year 2025. The agency is seeking to hire more examiners, but if high examiner attrition continues, it will affect the USPTO’s ability to reduce the backlog. As of August 2026, the 12-month examiner attrition rate was 7.6 percent.
The USPTO May Not Reach Its Backlog Goal Without Lowering Examiner Attrition
According to the stakeholders GAO interviewed, including the patent examiners’ union and former agency officials, the USPTO’s efforts to reduce the backlog may not be sustainable and could contribute to high attrition. Requiring examiners to review more applications and eliminating time for subject-matter training pose risks to the quality of examination. While the USPTO has expanded the use of AI tools, stakeholders told GAO these tools are not yet effective, because they do not reliably return useful patent search results. In addition, the USPTO paused a survey that provided the agency with stakeholder views on agency responsiveness and overall examination quality. Assessing and addressing risks to retention and examination quality could better position the USPTO to balance its efforts to reduce the backlog.
Why GAO Did This Study
The U.S. patent system encourages innovation by generally allowing a patent owner to exclude others from making, using, or selling patented inventions for up to 20 years. Patent examiners at the USPTO review applications to determine if the inventions meet legal patentability requirements.
The USPTO has long had a patent application backlog, and GAO reported in 2007 that the agency’s examiner hiring efforts were insufficient to address it. In recent years, the increase in the backlog has resulted in applicants waiting more than 20 months for an initial USPTO decision.
GAO was asked to review factors related to the patent application backlog at the USPTO. This report examines (1) the USPTO’s current goals and efforts to reduce the backlog and (2) what available data predict about the agency’s ability to achieve those goals, stakeholder views on these efforts, and the extent to which the USPTO assessed related risks.
GAO analyzed USPTO fiscal year 2020–2025 patent application and examiner data to estimate the future size of the backlog. GAO also analyzed federal workforce data on recent patent examiner attrition at the USPTO. GAO interviewed the patent examiners’ union, former USPTO officials, patent attorneys, trade associations, and researchers. GAO also sought information from the agency. The USPTO did not provide GAO with requested information.
